items.title: Fragmented Landscapes
items.author: Jason Kottke
items.content:
I don’t think it’s a surprise at this point when I tell you that I love these artworks by Antwerp-based artist Joost Vandebrug. (I mean, tell me they don’t aesthetically rhyme with the KDO logo circles/moons…)

Joost Vandebrug explores how separate views and moments come to be seen as a whole. His landscapes gather fragments into places that feel familiar, even when no single place could contain them. The image takes shape through remembering and looking, while the joins keep its construction visible.

Each work is built from dozens of photo-emulsion transfers on handmade paper cards. I transfer and reassemble them individually. Nothing is ever the same — every card has its imperfections. When I lay them together, they form a new landscape — part remembered, part reinvented.

Yeah, I love everything about this — the chunky pointillism, analog pixel art, small multiples, even Magic the Gathering vibes (if you think of the artworks as playable decks). Check out more of his work on his website and Instagram. Thanks to my pal Yen for the intro to his work; she snapped a photo of Vandebrug’s work in a gallery she visited recently.

items.title: The Rose by Jay DeFeo
items.author: Jason Kottke
items.content:
Jay DeFao’s The Rose is one of my favorite pieces at The Whitney (or anywhere really). The story of how this art world behemoth somehow survived to become of the jewels of American art is wild.

First exhibited in 1969, The Rose was taken to the San Francisco Art Institute, where it was covered with plaster for support and protection, and finally stored behind the wall of a conference room. Legend grew about the painting, but it remained sealed until 1995, when Whitney curator Lisa Phillips had it excavated and restored by a team of conservators, who created a backing strong enough to support the heavy paint.

items.title: The Energy Tax of Living in a New Place
items.author: Jason Kottke
items.content:
Before moving abroad, I was really independent. I loved socialising, visiting new places, trying new things. But over the past few years I’ve become so much more anxious and reserved, and I only just realised why.

When you live somewhere familiar, life is second nature. You know the language, the systems, the culture, and the social expectations. You have routines, support and things are predictable.

But when you live abroad, the energy required to participate in life increases. Socialising, going to appointments, buying a coffee, answering the phone. Everything requires so much more planning, energy and courage.

When you’re already mentally exhausted, you have less energy for the things you want and should do. You avoid situations that feel difficult. You become more reserved, less confident, more isolated and less independent.

I’m writing this at the airport after spending 2.5 months in Tokyo and feeling the above . I’ve never been what you’d call outgoing, but after the initial rush of being here wore off after a few weeks, I definitely noticed myself becoming “more reserved, less confident, more isolated and less independent”. Some days, I barely left my apartment because I couldn’t bear summoning the energy to make a plan, negotiate a new restaurant, or figure out how to get from point A to point B on the train. I sought out places that were easy: online ticketing, digital ordering screens, English menus, chain stores & restaurants.

The confidence piece is probably the hardest for me. I have to work hard in social situations with people I don’t know, and doing that in a language I don’t speak and in a cultural context I don’t fully understand is challenging, especially when I need to do it 10 times a day. I rely on humor in situations like these and, well, I don’t know how to be funny in Japan. Confidence tends to be a pervasive trait — a dip in one area of your life causes an overall decline across many areas. And all this is coming after living for the past decade in a place where I never felt like I fit in.

Anyway, it’s been eye-opening, this shift in energy & confidence. I’m onto the next place soon, but this is something I definitely need to keep an eye on.

items.title: What Happens to Your Body When You Die?
items.author: Jason Kottke
items.content:
Kurzgesagt explores what happens to your body when you die.

Death isn’t a single switch that shuts down your entire body at once. When your heart stops beating and your brain goes silent, trillions of cells inside you are still alive, desperately trying to keep themselves running. Death isn’t a single moment, but a slow and surprisingly complex process that can last for weeks.

What actually happens when you die? What makes death so mysterious, and which cells are the last survivors within your body?

items.title: Why Rich People Used To Collect Unicorn Horns
items.author: Jason Kottke
items.content:
During the Renaissance, spurred by the accelerating arrival of items from all over the world, wealthy Europeans began assembling handcrafted curios and unusual artifacts from the natural world in wonder cabinets, or wunderkammers. In this video, Evan Puschak takes a look at how this practice evolved and what it says about that period in history.

This was the period of the scientific revolution when thinkers were re-evaluating their reliance on ancient wisdom in the light of all the novel things arriving daily from around the world. “What grounds were there,” Steven Chapen writes, “for crediting ancient limits on the stock of factual knowledge? Every day, new phenomena presented themselves about which the ancient texts were silent.”

What was needed for the growth of real knowledge, according to philosophers like Francis Bacon, was not an interpretation of old texts, but an inventory of new facts.

A Web log really, then, is a Wunderkammer. That is to say, the genealogy of Web logs points not to the world of letters but to the early history of museums — to the “cabinet of wonders,” or Wunderkammer, that marked the scientific landscape of Renaissance modernity: a random collection of strange, compelling objects, typically compiled and owned by a learned, well-off gentleman. A set of ostrich feathers, a few rare shells, a South Pacific coral carving, a mummified mermaid — the Wunderkammer mingled fact and legend promiscuously, reflecting European civilization’s dazed and wondering attempts to assimilate the glut of physical data that science and exploration were then unleashing.

Just so, the Web log reflects our own attempts to assimilate the glut of immaterial data loosed upon us by the “discovery” of the networked world.

Some 26 years later, I still think about kottke.org that way. I mean, what is the Video Closet if not a cabinet of wonders?

items.title: Crime and Punishment in America
items.author: Jason Kottke
items.content:
Documentary filmmaker Lynn Novick, who co-directed The Vietnam War and The US and the Holocaust with Ken Burns, has directed an 8-hour PBS series called Crime and Punishment in America.

A sweeping look at the American criminal justice system, from the origins of prisons and policing to our continued fascination with crime, the film traces the contours of our imperfect system and how it influences nearly all parts of our society: the media, economics and politics. Through the voices and testimony of those who have committed crimes, experienced incarceration, enforced the law, or lost loved ones to violence, the series explores the cost of America’s choices and the enduring tension between crime and punishment, vengeance and mercy, justice and redemption.

We think about our history in terms of progress, but we have become consumed with practices of punishment.

When I think about crime and punishment in America, I think that it says we are a very unforgiving country.

This looks great. It starts airing on PBS tonight, Nov 16.

items.title: What Robert Caro Has Learned About Power
items.author: Jason Kottke
items.content:
Dwarkesh Patel recently interviewed Robert Caro for his podcast. They talked about loneliness, if JFK could have passed LBJ’s legislation, and how Caro gets people to talk. From the transcript:

Dwarkesh Patel: This raises another question that I wanted to ask you. You’re interviewing all these people, and in many cases, they must know that it’s not good for them to tell you what you want to know. In many cases, they tell you anyway. How do you get people to tell you things that they know they shouldn’t tell you?

Robert Caro: You ask terrific questions. Sometimes you’re sitting there and you know this person doesn’t want to talk to you about what you want to get out of them, like John Connally on how Johnson used money to get political power. I’m thinking, “But I’ve been through the notes. Connally collected the money and gave it out at Johnson’s instructions, so he’s the only guy who can tell me how Johnson did this, how he judged who to give money to.”

Sometimes Johnson would write on a request for money. If the guy asked for $1,500, Johnson would write, “Okay, 1,500.” Sometimes he’d write 500, sometimes he’d write no, but sometimes he’d write, “No, never.” I asked Connally what that meant, and he said, “This guy was never going to get money from Lyndon Johnson.” Then when you ask why he felt this way about this particular congressman, that’s when the really fascinating stories emerge.

Caro is 91 now, so every interview with him is a precious jewel, but one wonders if he’s got the time to finish that fifth LBJ book.

items.title: The Kottke.org Video Closet
items.author: Jason Kottke
items.content:
Ok folks, I’m gonna apologize in advance for totally ruining any plans you might have had for the rest of your day. This weekend I knocked together the Video Closet, a simple tool for exploring & watching every YouTube & Vimeo video I’ve posted to KDO since 2014 that’s still live: almost 5400 of them in total. It’s like a YouTube that’s just for people who read KDO. Click a video to play it or click the title to go to the original post containing the video.

The toughest thing about building the Video Closet was getting repeatedly distracted by videos while I was testing it. Seriously, don’t open this thing if you want to get any work done for the rest of the day!

I also tweaked how video embeds work on the main site: there’s now a play button (plays the video in place), an “open on [service]” button (opens it in a new tab on YT or Vimeo), and, on desktop browsers, a widescreen button that embiggens the video in the current window and plays it (my favorite). I like rolling my own video embeds because the default ones from YT & Vimeo are heavy and include a lot of tracking — and now you can choose three different ways of watching, according to the customs of your people.

items.title: A Literary Map of the United States
items.author: Jason Kottke
items.content:
There are many ways to read this map: as a peculiar road map of the United States, a potted history of the same, a metatext of American literature, a guide to American literary genres and their centers of gravity, and more. I will get to at least some of them later, but for now, I want to examine the effect that scholars call broadly “imaginative geography,” more precisely “toponymic capture,” and more elegantly “authorial inscription.” It is the process by which a writer’s vision of a place becomes so dominant that it effectively overwrites that place’s prior identity in the public imagination.

We could say other parts of America have been “colonized” by other texts the same way King’s horror stories have influenced our perception of Maine. A gentler metaphor, from Rebecca Solnit’s Infinite City, is of cultural and literary memory as an “overlay.” It resides above physical geography like a transparency on an overhead projector, a slightly shifting but persistent presence.

In Landmarks, the English nature writer Robert Macfarlane develops the idea that a sufficiently powerful text doesn’t just describe a landscape, but alters the mind that subsequently encounters it. He uses the verb phrase “to see through” to define it: you see the Suffolk coast through W.G. Sebald, the Mississippi through Mark Twain, the South (as a particularly “Gothic” place) through Faulkner.
